pr_title: stack: Do not add error if pop/shift/value accesses outside of the stack
pr_body:
This partially reverts commit 30eba7f35983a917f1007bce45040c0af3442e42.
This is legitimate use of the stack functions and no error should be reported apart from the NULL return value.

Fixes #19389

##### Checklist
<!-- Remove items that do not apply. For completed items, change [ ] to [x]. -->
- [x] tests are added or updated
pr_comments:
Actually even the stack == NULL cases should not report an error as seen by the previous test failure. 

@paulidale can you please reconfirm?

@DDvO I do not understand. I do not see what is contradicting in this patch with the sentence `sk_TYPE_pop(), sk_TYPE_shift(), sk_TYPE_delete() and sk_TYPE_delete_ptr() return a pointer to the deleted element or NULL on error` and not reporting error on error stack.

I am not saying we should actively encourage at least some of the sloppy uses of the stack functions however we should have never added the ERR_raise() calls that were added by the partially reverted commit.
It was my serious mistake that I did not recognize the problem when approving the commit that caused the regression.

> @DDvO I do not understand. I do not see what is contradicting in this patch with the sentence `sk_TYPE_pop(), sk_TYPE_shift(), sk_TYPE_delete() and sk_TYPE_delete_ptr() return a pointer to the deleted element or NULL on error` and not reporting error on error stack.

Well, at least to abstract datatype designers and many programmers including me, things like removing an element from an empty stack is an error (API abuse), and this is what also the existing documentation suggests.
Moreover, one should expect that errors are caught (as far as possible) and then also get reported.
Upon doing strange things, API users at least risk that they are "punished" by getting an error queue entry, and in the worst case even suffer a runtime crash.

Unfortunately, OpenSSL usually does not state under which conditions a function all may crash or at least under which conditions an element is added to the error queue.
 
> I am not saying we should actively encourage at least some of the sloppy uses of the stack functions however we should have never added the ERR_raise() calls that were added by the partially reverted commit.

How far backward compatible we should be at this point is a different question.
I can live with the status quo that was before commit 30eba7f35983a917f1007bce45040c0af3442e42 for the sake of backward compatibility,
but only if we point out in `DEFINE_STACK_OF.pod` which sloppy/wrong use is accepted (while better saying that it is discouraged) and do not continue to imply that these are error cases (since keeping them stated as errors would mean an inconsistency).
I disagree. IMO this PR should be merged without any documentation changes as it fixes a regression. If you want to add any documentation clarification afterwards, it can be done in a subsequent PR.

> we should have never added the ERR_raise() calls

Agreed.

The problem here is context. The stack structure doesn't know the context in which it's being used. It was obviously wrong to assume that error entries in from the stack structure would be part of the X509 library, but it's also wrong to assume that an error entry should be generated when processing an empty stack or a NULL stack pointer. That's really up to the caller to determine the context, and whether the condition is really an error or not. 

Utility APIs/simple data structures such as the stack should almost never create an error entry, with the possible exception of memory allocation. Even then, errors should be returned to the caller to generate an appropriate error entry (if at all) based on the context of their use.

(Trying to avoid the term "error stack" when we're talking about the stack structure, and also since this isn't C++, avoiding the idea of "throwing" an error.)

> Well, at least to abstract datatype designers and many programmers including me, things like removing an element from an empty stack is an error (API abuse)

Seen as a paradigm, there are different schools of thought on this.  Just looking at three languages' behavior makes that quite clear:

``` console
$ python3
Python 3.10.7 (main, Oct  1 2022, 04:31:04) [GCC 12.2.0] on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> a = [1]
>>> a.pop()
1
>>> a.pop()
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
IndexError: pop from empty list
>>> 
```

``` console
$ perl -e 'my @a = ( 1 ); print pop(@a), "\n"; print pop(@a), "\n"; print pop(@a), "\n";'
1


```
(popping from an empty list in perl returns `undef`, which is rendered with nothing)

``` console
$ clisp
...
[1]> (setq a '( 1 ))
(1)
[2]> (pop a)
1
[3]> (pop a)
NIL
[4]> (pop a)
NIL
```

In the case of python, the user can do the pop in a `try` construct, and be able to ignore the error. There would be no side effects.

BSD-queues (for C lang) do not spit out any errors or the like (no side effects). That's probably the closest equivalent to the OpenSSL stack.

In this current code, there are side effects (error entries being created), which is a change of behavior. The user would need to check and clear the error stack, possibly filtering them to see if there's a memory error, rather than a difference of opinion on how to use the API.

And my final point:

> sk_TYPE_pop(), sk_TYPE_shift(), sk_TYPE_delete() and sk_TYPE_delete_ptr() return a pointer to the deleted element or NULL on error.

An error return _does not_ necessarily require the side effect of an error entry. Lots of "errors" can occur that don't necessarily warrant the creation of an error entery.

I am fully in support of removing the side effect error entries. The user is still able to use the `OPENSSL_sk_num()` to determine if there are more than 1 entries, and then use `OPENSSL_sk_pop()` to get those entries, and generate an error entry if the pop fails.

The real error here would be if there _are_ entries in the stack and the pop/shift operation return NULL. Now, _that's_ worthy of an error entry, but that's not the case here.

> The real error here would be if there are entries in the stack and the pop/shift operation return NULL.

Not really. Note that it is technically legal to push a NULL pointer on the stack.
In such a case,
```
    STACK_OF(X509) *s = sk_X509_new_null();
    printf("res=%d\n", sk_X509_push(s, NULL));
    printf("num=%d\n", sk_X509_num(s));
    printf("pop=%p\n", (void*)sk_X509_pop(s));
```
yields
```
res=1
num=1
pop=(nil)
```
So from consulting the pop outcome, one cannot be sure whether NULL means an error or not.
In order to clearly distinguish a real error, one will have to call `sk_X509_num()` beforehand.
So at least in this (ok, extremely rare) corner case, the error queue entry would help.

In my view the error entry does help to detect inadvertently wrong (in the sense of sloppiness by mistake) use of the stack API.

Yet as mentioned, since people apparently prefer to be sloppy,  I wont't argue further against that. 
This way you deliberately take the risk of doing mistakes,
without the good chance of getting this signaled by an error entry.

I believe that these low level data structures should handle bad inputs gracefully.  Either by raising errors or doing something sensible.  I don't see adding errors here as a regression.  The regression is not fixing _all_ the callers to deal with it -- i.e. don't pass bad values in and check before (or after) doing operations that could fail, cleaning up appropriately.

So your argumentation boils down to backward compatibility with IMHO bad practice.

It all depends on what one sees as genuine error or not, which indeed is debatable.
Though, as mentioned, there are pretty clear indications even in the existing documentation
that things like `sk_TYPE_pop(NULL)` are considered an error.

It was never documented that such cases do not lead to an error queue entry,
so callers cannot rely on not getting such an entry.

> @DDvO how would you fix similar "problems" with stack usage in 3rd party code???

It is their responsibility to clean up their code, and they should be glad to finally get a hint that something is fishy in their code!
I actually had this experience myself as a follow-up to my improvements contributed in #18918,
namely in the securityUtilities library: https://github.com/siemens/libsecutils/pull/36

And even when removing all the new error queue additions,
there is no need to revert the various improvements to the sloppy stack API uses I did in commit 30eba7f35983a917f1007bce45040c0af3442e42 .

A closer inspection of the `OPENSSL_sk_` API seems to show that it was designed to be forgiving.
An indicator is that all the `OPENSSL_sk_find()` variants return -1 when the value couldn't be found (something I wouldn't consider an error!) as well as for "invalid" input (such as `st == NULL`); raising an error record in one case but not the other would be confusing, but raising an error record in both cases would be questionable (at least if you agree that it's not an error if the value wasn't found).
Another indicator is that `OPENSSL_sk_zero()` is a void function and can therefore not give an indication that there was something wrong (*And why the hell you'd choose to raise an error record there is beyond me to fathom!*).

Another thing one might observe is that the effort of raising more error records is only half done.  There are plenty of `OPENSSL_sk_` functions that raise nothing when `sk == NULL` (or `st == NULL` as the case may be), just as an example (and like I said, that would be confusing for `OPENSSL_sk_find` functions).

I'd like to add a voice to support for removing the error entry on out-of-bounds accesses. The behavior change in the stable branch came to me as a surprise.

FWIW, in the <= 1.0.2 era, doc/ssleay.txt was the only place where `sk_{delete,pop,shift}()` were documented. It didn't explicitly specify such cases as an error.

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/d2a0d72f33e2cd81a5c81b29b05d6fdb2cc67ac2/doc/ssleay.txt#L6662-L6694

> A closer inspection of the `OPENSSL_sk_` API seems to show that it was designed to be forgiving. An indicator is that all the `OPENSSL_sk_find()` variants return -1 when the value couldn't be found (something I wouldn't consider an error!) as well as for "invalid" input (such as `st == NULL`); raising an error record in one case but not the other would be confusing, but raising an error record in both cases would be questionable (at least if you agree that it's not an error if the value wasn't found). Another indicator is that `OPENSSL_sk_zero()` is a void function and can therefore not give an indication that there was something wrong (_And why the hell you'd choose to raise an error record there is beyond me to fathom!_).

To me, these are not indications of deliberate design but just just examples of sloppy/erroneous implementation with confusing effects.
For instance, `sk_TYPE_find(NULL, x)` should be an error, while calling it with an empty stack is of course fine.

> FWIW, in the <= 1.0.2 era, doc/ssleay.txt was the only place where `sk_{delete,pop,shift}()` were documented. It didn't explicitly specify such cases as an error.

In the <= 1.0.2 era, these were probably meant to be quite internal...  unfortunately, this is too far back, my recollection of that time is a bit vague these days.

> I'd like to add a voice to support for removing the error entry on out-of-bounds accesses. The behavior change in the stable branch came to me as a surprise.

It is not uncommon that being pointed out an error hits you as surprise.
Hopefully you take this as a positive surprise and fix your code,
rather than argumenting against the error report or closing your eyes on it.

> For instance, `sk_TYPE_find(NULL, x)` should be an error, while calling it with an empty stack is of course fine.

Yes, and in both cases, -1 is returned.

> > For instance, `sk_TYPE_find(NULL, x)` should be an error, while calling it with an empty stack is of course fine.
> 
> Yes, and in both cases, -1 is returned.

So my proposal is to fix all the remaining `sk_TYPE_*()` inconsistencies as well (as far as possible without clear API breaks, of course).

The other thing to do is to go in all parts of our code and add checks...  from what #19389 indicates, some checks are still not in place.  There are quite a few places to look at:

``` console
$ git grep -P 'sk_[a-zA-Z0-9_]*_(delete|shift|pop|zero|value|set)' -- apps crypto/ ssl engines/ providers/ demos/ test/ | grep -v '^crypto/stack/' | wc -l
1135
```

Also, if we want to be complete, there are quite a few `OPENSSL_sk_` functions that do not raise any error record at all, even though they check the same sort of condition (`st == NULL`).  *(and oh, be careful if you go ahead and do this...  for some functions, for example `OPENSSL_sk_dup()`, `st == NULL` **is valid input!**)*

I really do not want to go there! The API was designed to be forgiving and it should stay so. It is public API. This is my final comment on this matter. If we want an unforgiving stack API we will have to add a new one. Not that I think it would be worth it.
Either way, *please* change `ERR_LIB_X509` to `ERR_LIB_CRYPTO`.  (unless this PR is accepted)

> I really do not want to go there! The API was designed to be forgiving and it should stay so. It is public API. This is my final comment on this matter. If we want an unforgiving stack API we will have to add a new one. Not that I think it would be worth it.

Looks like this would be worth an OTC decision.
IMO if the outcome is to stick with the forgiving 'design' (better to say: legacy), this should imply fixing the so far pretty spotty `sk_TYPE` documentation by making explicit which input corner cases are accepted but not encouraged.
It's always ok to make the documentation more correct visavi the implementation.  That seems to always be needed :wink:

> It's always ok to make the documentation more correct visavi the implementation. That seems to always be needed wink

I'd say that in particular for such a heavily used API, 
no matter how good/sloppy its implementation is,
its not only okay, but actually _mandatory_
to fix the existing omissions (and any inconsistencies) in its documentation.

> > It's always ok to make the documentation more correct visavi the implementation. That seems to always be needed wink
> 
> I'd say that in particular for such a heavily used API, no matter how good/sloppy its implementation is, its not only okay, but actually _mandatory_ to fix the existing omissions (and any inconsistencies) in its documentation.

Yes, sure...  I'm just trying to be encouraging, but I can do that with the usual mantra too: PR welcome!

> @paulidale No, these are public interfaces! We cannot blindly add error raises to these.

We can.  We've long established that **adding** errors does not constitute an API break.
Removing them **is** an API break.

These APIs were not originally designed to be forgiving, the safety checks came later in little pieces and still do not cover all functions.  Likewise, even after this PR, there are some calls that raise errors when passed bad arguments.

We need to make this consistent.  Either:
* all functions should validate all their arguments to make the library safe or
* they should validate their arguments and raise errors.

Given that some pre-existing calls check their arguments and raise errors and that we cannot remove these outside of a major release, I think adding errors is the better path forwards.
Then raise hold: needs otc decision. Because I disagree.
OTC: **which way forward?**

> These APIs were not originally designed to be forgiving, 

After having been there with no error recording for about 20 years (and that doesn't include the time it was sitting around in OpenSSL's ancestor SSLeay), I'm not sure we can say neither this nor that about the original design.  Truly.
(the first time an error record was added to the `OPENSSL_sk` API was in 2018, with commit fe1128dc2a6e7aae9010cf6595c78245e0eefd46).

> the safety checks came later in little pieces and still do not cover all functions.

... which is quite sloppy as well...

> Likewise, even after this PR, there are some calls that raise errors when passed bad arguments.

True that.  
> We need to make this consistent. Either:
> 
>     * all functions should validate all their arguments to make the library safe or
> 
>     * they should validate their arguments and raise errors.

I'm not sure what's the difference between validating arguments and validating arguments, but I do agree with needing to make it more consistent.  *(and we still need to consider what to do with the `OPENSSL_sk_find` functions, and not record an error in void functions like `OPENSSL_sk_zero()`)*

> Given that some pre-existing calls check their arguments and raise errors and that we cannot remove these outside of a major release, I think adding errors is the better path forwards.

*AND* get through all the places where we call the stack functions, across all our code, so we don't get ourselves in the situation shown in #19389!  That's quite a chunk.
Added the requested documentation.

24 hours has passed since 'approval: done' was set, but as this PR has been updated in that time the label 'approval: ready to merge' is not being automatically set.  Please review the updates and set the label manually.
This does not need a OTC hold. The regression needs to be removed ASAP. If there is another PR later that wishes to address this again, then that could have a OTC hold on it.

@slontis, I disagree about the hold, I do not believe that a consensus will be reached in this discussion.
I definitely agree that this needs to be addressed quickly.

The question seems to boil down to:
* Should the raised errors be removed?  Breaking our 3.0.6 API guarantee.  We've no policy about API changes in withdrawn releases.  Adding errors isn't considered a breaking change, removing them is.  Errors were added in 3.0.6.
* Should the calling code deal with the raised errors appropriately?  Maintaining the 3.0.6 API and fixing the regression.

The followup is what should we do with the stack code going forward: add errors universally, not have errors universally or simply don't check.  The current state is a hodgepodge.

So we do need policies related to this kind of thing, but I don't think we should be waiting for weeks before another release is done. If someone is relying on error stacks from a release that got retracted after a day, then that seems like a silly argument.
On a related note the 3.0.4 release should have also be withdrawn - this one is a bit trickier since it has been in the released state for quite a while. (It may be too late to remove it now?).

In order to take the immediate pressure out of #19389, I've just fixed it in #19414 
in the most straightforward way: removing a sloppy use of the stack API in `p12_kiss.c`.
We should not start to add things on the error queue for a function that previously never did in a stable release.

> We should not start to add things on the error queue for a function that previously never did in a stable release.

This, I think is key. Very well put, @kroeckx!
It's very apparent that what was done with these stack functions didn't just add an error report, it became a deeper shift of behaviour, in a way that we missed, but that becomes very clear with all the surrounding changes that are needed, but most of all, that we don't even agree what is actually an error or what should be acceptable.

Live an learn...

**OTC vote has passed to allow this subject to normal review process.**
https://github.com/openssl/technical-policies/issues/56
Actually this still needs OTC approval as @paulidale's approval was stale.
This pull request is ready to merge
Merged to master and 3.0 branches. Thank you for the reviews.

issue_context.title: PKCS12_parse leaves errors on stack [3.0.6]
issue_context.body: OpenSSL 3.0.6 has a regression where successful parse of a PKCS12 via `PKCS12_parse` leaves errors on the stack. This appears to be due to changes to error handling in functions that `PKCS12_parse` calls.
comments:
It's because of https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/openssl-3.0/crypto/pkcs12/p12_kiss.c#L92

shift was changed to put an error on the stack if you shfit from an enpty stack

this regression is trivially observed by running the pyca/cryptography test suite
@reaperhulk - Does this mean that the external tests that we have for pyca are older than the ones we currently have? Any chance this could be updated?

Your external tests are not properly configured. Looking at a recent job from the 3.0 branch: https://github.com/openssl/openssl/actions/runs/3226931046/jobs/5281077558

> OpenSSL: OpenSSL 1.1.1f  31 Mar 2020

You are linking pyca/cryptography against a system OpenSSL, not the OpenSSL you have built.

It's also the case that your copy of pyca/cryptography is a year old, but that's not relevant here.
Has this been broken since it got put in (6 years ago)

@alex Isnt the -L option supposed to handle this?
i.e.
````
CFLAGS=-I/home/runner/work/openssl/openssl/test-runs/test_external_pyca/../../include -I/home/runner/work/openssl/openssl/test-runs/test_external_pyca/../../include -L/home/runner/work/openssl/openssl/test-runs/test_external_pyca/../.. pytest -n auto tests --wycheproof-root=../wycheproof
````

> Has this been broken since it got put in (6 years ago)

AFAIK no, at some point it was definitely linking to the openssl being built.

> It's because of https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/openssl-3.0/crypto/pkcs12/p12_kiss.c#L92
> shift was changed to put an error on the stack if you shfit from an enpty stack

Very sorry for my oversight.

> Fix in #19400

Alternative direct fix is in #19414.

review_comments:
Note that these changes essentially collapse `OPENSSL_sk_delete()` into `internal_delete()`.
It looks to me that the distinction between the two functions was that `OPENSSL_sk_delete()` provides not only error detection, but also error reporting.
I do not think so. The internal delete is without error checking completely and it should stay so.

I disagree with reverting such cleanups of sloppy stack API uses that were done in  https://github.com/openssl/openssl/commit/30eba7f35983a917f1007bce45040c0af3442e42.

Going back to `while ((sct = sk_SCT_pop(src)) != NULL)` does not contribute to fixing the small regression reported in #19389, and in IMO would be even counter-productive and promote a questionable coding style.
And I disagree with this as if the sk_pop on empty stack is legitimate call, and I insist that it is, there is nothing wrong with it to be used across the code.

At least the following _is_ wrong/problematic with `while ((sct = sk_SCT_pop(src)) != NULL)`:
it does not distinguish between NULL entries on the stack, the empty stack, and a NULL stack pointer.
I'd prefer these to remain, however I can live with removing them for the moment.  They can be reintroduced separately.
Wow, the error subsystem shouldn't have been X509, to begin with!
